chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Life of an ESOP

lessons.title: ESOP Pools and ESOP Trusts: Where the Shares Come From

children.text: When you exercise an option, shares have to come from somewhere. Either the company creates new ones, which makes every existing owner’s slice slightly smaller, or a trust hands over shares it already holds. That choice, made years before you join, shapes how quickly your options can turn into something real.

body.text: An ESOP pool is not a pot of money. It is a reserved block of ownership, carved out of somebody’s stake, and the negotiation over whose stake it comes from happens before a single employee is hired.

children.text: The Pool: Ownership Set Aside in Advance
An
ESOP pool

is a number of shares reserved for employees and approved by shareholders. Grants are made out of it, and nothing can be granted beyond it. When the pool empties, the company must go back to shareholders for a
top-up

markDefs.definition: The block of shares a company sets aside exclusively for employee options. Nothing can be granted beyond what the pool holds.
An increase in the size of the ESOP pool, usually approved alongside a funding round when the existing pool runs low.

stats.label: Pre-seed or bootstrapped
stats.context: A handful of early hires, each taking a meaningful slice

stats.label: Seed stage
stats.context: Commonly set or topped up at the seed round

stats.label: Series A and beyond
stats.context: Often higher again at late stage, where refresh grants run continuously

children.text: These are market norms, not rules. What matters more than the headline percentage is how much of the pool is still unallocated, which is the question almost no candidate asks.
Who Actually Pays for the Pool
Here is the part that surprises founders. Investors almost always insist the pool be created on a
pre-money
basis, which means the pool is carved out of the existing shareholders before the new money is counted. The investor’s percentage is protected. The founders absorb it.

markDefs.definition: A pool created before the new investment is counted, so the dilution falls on existing shareholders rather than the incoming investor.

children.text: Take a company with 10,00,000 shares: Founder A holds 60%, Founder B 30%, and an angel 10%. A Series A investor puts in ₹20 crore for 20% post-money, and requires a 10% pool to exist at closing.

body.caption: Series A with a 10% pre-money ESOP pool

body.title: Pre-money pool vs post-money pool, in one comparison

children.text: Founder A went from 60% to 42%. The investment alone would have taken her to 48%, since 60% of the remaining 80% is 48%. The extra six percentage points are the pool, paid for entirely by the existing shareholders.
Had the pool been created post-money, it would have diluted everyone including the new investor. Founder A would have held about 43.2% and the investor 18% instead of 20%.

This single line in a term sheet is worth more than most of the clauses founders spend time arguing about. It is standard market practice, but it is negotiable in size, and a founder who can show a credible hiring plan can often justify a smaller pool.

body.title: Whose Dilution Is It?
body.question: A term sheet says the company must have a 12% ESOP pool on a pre-money, fully diluted basis at closing. Who bears the dilution of creating that pool?
options: The incoming investor, since they asked for it
The existing shareholders, mainly the founders
It is shared equally between old and new shareholders
body.explanation: Pre-money means the pool exists before the new money is counted, so it comes out of the existing cap table. The investor still receives exactly the percentage they negotiated. This is the most consequential and least discussed line in a Series A term sheet.

body.title: Name the Basis
body.textWithBlank: When an ESOP pool is created on a ___ money basis, the dilution falls on the existing shareholders rather than on the incoming investor.
body.explanation: Pre-money pool creation is the market standard in Indian venture rounds. Founders should model its effect on their own stake before agreeing to the pool size.

children.text: Reading the Pool Like an Insider
The headline pool size tells you almost nothing on its own. What matters is what is left. Here is the same
fully diluted
cap table a year later, with a pool of 1,00,000 options.

markDefs.definition: The total share count assuming every option, convertible and reserved share becomes an ordinary share. It is the honest denominator for any ownership percentage.

body.caption: Pool status after a year of hiring

cells: Promised, though mostly unvested so far
Already real shares held by employees
From leavers, back into the pool for reuse
What the company can actually offer you today

body.title: How Much Is Left?
body.prompt: A company approved a pool of 1,00,000 options, has granted 60,000, and 5,000 options have lapsed from leavers and returned to the pool. How many options can it still grant?
body.explanation: 1,00,000 minus 60,000 plus 5,000 = 45,000 options. Note that exercised options are a subset of granted ones, not a separate deduction.

children.text: What your own grant is worth as a percentage

At a post-money valuation of ₹100 crore across 10,00,000 fully diluted shares, each share is worth ₹1,000. An employee granted 5,000 options holds 0.5% of the company fully diluted, a gross value of ₹50,00,000, or ₹49,50,000 net of a ₹10 exercise price at today’s valuation.

body.text: Always ask for your grant as a percentage of fully diluted shares, not just a number of options. "5,000 options" means nothing until you know whether the company has 10 lakh shares or 10 crore.

children.text: The Trust Route: Shares Held on Your Behalf
Instead of issuing new shares each time someone exercises, a company can set up an
ESOP trust
. The trust holds shares, funded either by a fresh issue from the company or by
secondary acquisition
, and transfers them to employees when options are exercised.

markDefs.definition: A separate legal entity that holds shares on behalf of a company’s employee benefit schemes and transfers them to employees on exercise.
The purchase of existing shares from current holders, rather than the issue of new shares by the company.

columns.label: Direct issue by the company
points: New shares are created at each exercise, diluting holders then
Simpler and cheaper to set up, so most startups begin here
Every exercise needs board allotment and filings
Shares come straight from the company to the employee

columns.label: Through an ESOP trust
points: The trust holds shares in advance and simply transfers them
Dilution happens once, when the trust is funded
Can buy back shares from leavers and recycle them
More structure, trustees and compliance to maintain

children.text: For listed companies the trust route is tightly regulated under the SEBI SBEB and Sweat Equity Regulations, 2021, because a trust buying its own company’s shares in the market could otherwise be used to influence the price.

body.label: Secondary acquisition limit for a listed company’s ESOP trust
body.context: Capped at 2% of paid-up equity capital in a financial year, and 5% in aggregate across all share-based schemes, with a minimum holding period and restrictions on who may be a trustee.

children.text: Trustees
cannot be promoters or key managerial personnel of the company.
Shares held by the trust
cannot be voted at the trustees’ discretion, so the trust cannot become a friendly voting block.
A minimum holding period
applies to shares the trust acquires from the market.

body.text: If your employer runs a trust, ask who funds it. A trust with no shares and no funding is an administrative shell, and your options still depend on a fresh issue whenever you exercise.

body.title: Sizing the Pool Before a Round
body.scenario: Nikhil founded a 30-person edtech company in Pune. His existing pool is 6%, of which only 0.8% remains unallocated. A Series A investor wants a 14% pool on a pre-money basis at closing. Nikhil must hire a VP of Engineering, a VP of Sales and about 25 people over the next 18 months.
body.prompt: How should he approach the pool discussion, and what is the trade-off?
body.modelAnswer: He should build the number from the hiring plan rather than argue percentages in the abstract. Two VP-level hires might need 1% to 2% each, and 25 employees at an average of 0.15% is roughly 3.75%, so the plan justifies somewhere near 7% of new grants on top of the 5.2% already granted, which lands close to the investor number but with evidence behind it. The trade-off is direct: every extra point of pre-money pool comes out of his and his co-founders’ stake, not the investor’s. If the investor holds firm at 14%, two fair counters are to size the pool for 12 months of hiring with a committed top-up at the next round, or to ask that any pool increase above the agreed plan be created post-money so the investor shares the dilution. He should also ask for unallocated pool shares to be treated consistently in the price per share calculation, since the pool size directly affects what the investor pays per share.

cards.definition: Shares reserved for employee grants, approved by shareholders.
Share count assuming all options and convertibles become shares. The honest denominator.
A pool created before the new investment counts, diluting only existing holders.
An increase in the pool, usually approved alongside a funding round.
An entity holding shares on behalf of the scheme, transferring them to employees on exercise.
Buying existing shares rather than issuing new ones. Capped at 2% a year for listed company trusts.

points: An ESOP pool is reserved ownership, and grants can never exceed it.
Indian pools run about 5% to 8% pre-seed, 10% to 12% at seed and 12% to 15% at Series A, as market practice rather than rule.
Pools are usually created pre-money, so founders and existing shareholders bear the dilution while the investor keeps their agreed percentage.
Ask how much of the pool is unallocated, not just how large it is.
Lapsed options from leavers return to the pool and can be granted again.
Ask for your grant as a percentage of fully diluted shares, since a raw option count means nothing without the denominator.
A trust holds shares in advance and recycles them; for listed companies its market purchases are capped at 2% of capital a year and 5% in aggregate.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Cap table figures are illustrative and deliberately rounded. Pool norms vary by sector, stage and investor, and trust structures carry legal and compliance requirements that need professional advice.
